summary: This RFC specifies the protocols and procedures a service provider uses so IP multicast traffic inside a BGP/MPLS IP VPN can travel from one VPN site to another. It is the core description of multicast VPNs on that kind of network.

eli5.summary: A company has offices far apart on a private network. This describes how one message can be sent to many offices at once, across the provider's network, without everything being copied separately.

questions: how does multicast work over mpls vpn
subtitle: How a provider carries a customer's IP multicast between VPN sites without drowning its core routers in per-flow state.

tldr.problem: BGP/MPLS IP VPNs carry unicast between customer sites but have no way to carry IP multicast, and optimal multicast routing would force core routers to hold state for every customer flow.
tldr.mechanism: PE routers discover each other with BGP, exchange customer multicast routing with PIM or BGP, and carry the traffic over provider tunnels (PMSIs) that can be shared by many VPNs or narrowed to a few receivers.
tldr.outcome: A provider can trade multicast optimality against core state and pick tunnel technologies per its needs. RFC 6513 is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 7582, RFC 7900 and RFC 7988.

today: RFC 6513 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2012 and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 7582, RFC 7900 and RFC 7988. For anything about BGP encodings, read it together with RFC 6514.

sections.title: Adding Multicast to BGP/MPLS IP VPNs
sections.content:
RFC 4364 defines the service a provider offers as a BGP/MPLS IP VPN. It lets IP unicast packets travel from one customer site to another, but it gives no way for IP multicast traffic to do the same. RFC 6513 extends that service so it also handles multicast. A VPN that does is called a Multicast VPN, or MVPN.

Several protocols have to work together, so the document is partly a framework and partly a detailed specification. Some protocols are specified elsewhere. For anything about BGP, the companion document RFC 6514 is the authoritative one if the two ever disagree.

The customer side stays as close to the unicast model as possible. A customer edge router (CE) becomes a multicast routing neighbor of its provider edge router (PE), and CEs at different sites never become neighbors of each other. The multicast protocol on the PE-CE link is presumed to be PIM, in its any-source (ASM) and source-specific (SSM) service models, including the bidirectional variant. PIM dense mode is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The phone company already knew how to carry private one-to-one calls between your offices. This memo teaches it to carry one-to-many announcements too, in a way that keeps each company's traffic private.

sections.title: Optimality Versus Scalability
sections.content:
In a unicast VPN the provider's core (P) routers keep no per-VPN state. They only need routes to the PEs, so their state depends on the number of PEs, not the number of VPNs. Multicast is harder. Routing a flow optimally means the P routers on its path hold state specific to that flow, a flow being a (source, group) pair. The provider cannot control how many groups, senders or receivers its customers have, so that state could grow without bound.

The RFC therefore lets the provider trade optimality against scalability, and even choose per group. There are three main options:

  • Inclusive tree: one tree in the backbone carries all multicast traffic for a set of one or more MVPNs and reaches every PE in them. Several MVPNs can share a tree (an Aggregate Inclusive Tree), so state no longer grows with the number of MVPNs. The cost is that some PEs receive data they do not need.
  • Selective tree: a tree for only certain groups, reaching only the PEs that need them. It is more optimal but needs more state in the P routers. The text suggests high bandwidth groups as candidates.
  • Ingress replication: the ingress PE copies each packet and unicasts a copy through a tunnel to every egress PE that needs it. There is no multicast state in the P routers at all, but the ingress PE carries the whole copying load.
sections.eli5: Imagine a teacher passing out a handout. She can hand a copy to every student in the school (simple, but wasteful), only to the classes that want it (smarter, but she must keep a list), or walk to each desk herself (no list in the hallway, but a lot of walking).

sections.title: PMSIs and P-Tunnels
sections.content:
The central idea is the P-Multicast Service Interface (PMSI). It is a conceptual overlay on the provider network: a PE in an MVPN hands a packet to the PMSI, and the packet is delivered to some or all of the other PEs in that MVPN, each of which can tell which MVPN it belongs to. The transport mechanism that actually realises a PMSI is a P-tunnel. Keeping the service and its implementation apart lets the RFC discuss them separately.

There are three kinds of PMSI. A Multidirectional Inclusive PMSI (MI-PMSI) lets any PE reach every other PE of the MVPN, like an overlay broadcast network, and there is at most one per MVPN. A Unidirectional Inclusive PMSI (UI-PMSI) does the same from one particular PE, at most one per PE per MVPN. A Selective PMSI (S-PMSI) reaches only a subset of the PEs, and there can be any number per PE per MVPN.

P-tunnels can be built with PIM trees, mLDP point-to-multipoint or multipoint-to-multipoint LSPs, RSVP-TE point-to-multipoint LSPs, or a mesh of unicast tunnels. The choice belongs to the sending router and is local policy, but any technique a PE uses for an MVPN is expected to be supported by all the other PEs of that MVPN. If any PE uses ingress replication for an MVPN, all the others MUST too. The RFC states that the conditions under which a given tree-building method is applicable are outside its scope.
sections.eli5: A PMSI is like a promise: if you drop a message in the slot, the right offices will get it and know which company it is for. A P-tunnel is the actual delivery truck that keeps that promise.

sections.title: Discovery and Customer Multicast Routing
sections.content:
Before PEs can exchange anything they must find each other. BGP auto-discovery uses a new address family, MCAST-VPN. Each PE attached to an MVPN originates an Intra-AS I-PMSI auto-discovery route whose NLRI carries the route type, the originating PE's IP address and a locally configured route distinguisher. It carries Route Target extended communities, which tell receivers which MVPN the PE belongs to, and often a PMSI Tunnel attribute naming the tunnel technology, a tunnel identifier and, if the tunnel can be shared, a demultiplexor value. The encodings are specified in RFC 6514.

Next, a PE must pass the customer's Join/Prune information to other PEs. It first has to find the Upstream Multicast Hop for the source or rendezvous point, normally by looking up the root in the VRF. The default rule that MUST be implemented picks the candidate whose upstream PE address is numerically highest. A hash-based alternative that spreads load across equal-cost paths MUST also be implemented but is off by default.

Two ways of exchanging the routing information are described. With full PIM peering, the MI-PMSI is treated as a LAN, PEs form ordinary PIM adjacencies over it, and customer PIM packets go to 224.0.0.13 encapsulated in the P-tunnel, so P routers never process them. With BGP, MCAST-VPN routes for source tree joins and shared tree joins replace PE-to-PE Join/Prune messages. BGP updates do not provide explicit tracking of who joined, because that costs state; where it is needed, PEs use Leaf A-D routes instead.
sections.eli5: First the offices have to find out who else is in the club, and they do that by posting notices on a shared board. Then they tell each other who wants which show, either by talking directly or by leaving messages on that board.

sections.title: Carrying Data: Tunnels, Aggregation and S-PMSIs
sections.content:
When many MVPNs share one P-tunnel, the egress PE needs a way to tell them apart. The RFC uses an MPLS label that the ingress PE assigns itself (an upstream-assigned label) and announces in BGP. It sits just beneath the label identifying the tree, and the egress PE looks it up in a label space specific to that ingress PE. The egress PE MUST NOT advertise Implicit or Explicit Null for such a tree. Aggregation is optional, and the RFC does not mandate any rule for deciding which MVPNs to aggregate. It does note the trade-off: the less the member sites overlap, the more unwanted traffic PEs receive.

A customer flow can be bound to a specific P-tunnel, for example to move a busy flow off an inclusive tree onto a selective one. Only the PE that transmits the flow decides. When it moves a flow from one tunnel to another it MUST wait for a configurable switch-over delay and then send on the new tunnel only, never on both. Two protocols announce the binding. One uses BGP S-PMSI A-D routes. The other is a UDP-based protocol: an S-PMSI Join message is sent periodically over the MI-PMSI to 224.0.0.13, UDP port 3232.

The Type 1 S-PMSI Join covers an IPv4 customer flow carried on a PIM tunnel. Its defaults are a 3 second delay before using the new tunnel, a 3 minute timeout after which a receiver prunes itself, a 1 minute holdown before the sender falls back to an inclusive tunnel, and a 60 second send interval. With ingress replication it is recommended that explicit tracking be used, so each flow is sent only to PEs that need it.
sections.eli5: When lots of companies share one delivery truck, each parcel gets a sticker saying which company it is for. And if one parcel is huge, the sender can switch it to its own truck, waiting a few seconds first so nobody gets two copies.

sections.title: Inter-AS Operation and Duplicate Prevention
sections.content:
An MVPN can have sites in more than one autonomous system. The RFC describes two kinds of inter-AS P-tunnel. A segmented tunnel is a chain of independent intra-AS segments stitched together at the border routers (ASBRs), with one-hop unicast tunnels between ASes, so each AS can use its own technology. A non-segmented tunnel is a single tunnel spanning the ASes, so every AS on the path must support its technology. For non-segmented trees the Intra-AS I-PMSI A-D routes MUST be distributed across AS boundaries, and PIM joins carry a new MVPN Join attribute with a proxy address (the next ASBR toward the upstream PE) and a route distinguisher, so trees can be built even when ASBRs and P routers have no route to the upstream PE. The segmented procedures are in RFC 6514.

Duplicate packets are the other big concern. An egress PE can receive more than one copy when a source or rendezvous point is multihomed to several PEs, or when receivers switch from the shared tree to a source tree. Every MVPN MUST use at least one of three methods: discard packets that arrive from the wrong PE, allow only a single forwarder (the default upstream PE) to send into the backbone, or rely on native PIM mechanisms such as Assert and Prune(S,G,rpt). With BGP routing and both shared and source trees, the RFC adds Source Active A-D routes, so that PEs stop sending a source's traffic toward PEs on the shared tree once others have moved to the source tree.

Two optional features reduce state further. Sections 10.1 and 10.2 let PEs learn active sources, either by acting as anycast rendezvous points or by running MSDP with a local rendezvous point, so that shared tree state need not be passed between PEs. Section 11 covers bidirectional PIM groups, either by treating the whole backbone as the rendezvous point link or by partitioning the PEs and tagging packets with a PE Distinguisher Label.
sections.eli5: When offices are in different countries, the delivery has to cross borders, either as one long trip or as relay legs. And the post office must make sure nobody gets the same letter twice, for example by letting only one sender in a pair actually mail it.

sections.title: Encapsulations
sections.content:
Customer packets are wrapped for the trip across the provider network. For a P-tunnel carrying a single PMSI the options are GRE, IP-in-IP and MPLS. With GRE the outer IP protocol number MUST be 47 and the GRE protocol type is 0x800 or 0x86dd for an IPv4 or IPv6 customer packet. With IP-in-IP the protocol (or Next Header) value is 4 or 41 for the same two cases. For an MPLS LSP, penultimate-hop-popping MUST be disabled.

When several PMSIs share a P-tunnel, the encapsulations use an upstream-assigned MPLS label for demultiplexing, so MPLS-in-GRE and MPLS-in-IP are used instead. The GRE protocol type MUST then be 0x8847. A packet on a multipoint-to-multipoint LSP carrying a unidirectional customer tree MUST carry a second label that identifies its ingress PE, because the receiving PE could not tell otherwise.

General rules for IP and GRE tunnels: the encapsulating router MUST set the DF bit in the outer header, and the originator of a customer packet is responsible for making it small enough to arrive. The ingress PE should not copy the TTL from the customer header. If PIM trees are used for the provider network, the group addresses used for MVPN must be distinct from the provider's Internet multicast groups, best done with administratively scoped addresses.
sections.eli5: Customer packets travel inside an outer envelope, like a letter in a bigger package. The package label says which kind of delivery it is, and the package must never be chopped up on the way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This work extends RFC 4364 and shares its security considerations, along with those of RFC 4365. The security considerations of the other protocols used (PIM, BGP, mLDP and RSVP-TE) apply too.

The RFC adds several specific rules. A P or PE router MUST make sure that PIM, mLDP or RSVP-TE control messages building P-tunnels come from another P or PE router, not from a CE. A PE MUST NOT accept MCAST-VPN BGP routes from a CE. An S-PMSI Join (UDP port 3232, sent to 224.0.0.13) that does not arrive over a PMSI is illegal and MUST be dropped. By default an ASBR MUST NOT let P-tunnels extend beyond AS boundaries, because without an agreement between providers that could be an attempt to intercept data, though it MUST be configurable on chosen interfaces.

Because the network keeps state proportional to customer multicast activity, unexpected customer activity could overload P and PE routers. An implementation SHOULD let the provider limit the number of customer multicast states per VRF, the number of S-PMSI P-tunnels per VRF, and the number of P-tunnels through a given P router. Implementations of the active-source procedures MUST be able to bound how many Source Active A-D routes are generated and how often.
sections.eli5: The rules are about not letting strangers sneak into the delivery system. Messages that set up trucks must come from the post office's own staff, not from a customer, and the post office needs a way to say stop if one customer asks for too much.

fields.desc: Should be zero when sent and ignored on receipt.

fields.desc: IPv4 address of the traffic source in the VPN.

fields.name: C-group
fields.desc: IPv4 multicast destination address in the VPN.

fields.name: P-group
fields.desc: IPv4 group address the PE uses to encapsulate the flow.

viz.caption: S-PMSI JOIN TIMERS AND THEIR DEFAULTS (RFC 6513)

items.label: 3 seconds
items.desc: Sender waits this long after the Join before using the S-PMSI.

items.label: 3 minutes
items.desc: Receiver prunes itself if no packets arrive on the S-PMSI for this long.

items.label: 1 minute
items.desc: Sender returns to an I-PMSI if it sees no packets for this long.

items.label: 60 seconds
items.desc: How often the sender repeats the Join message.

viz.caption: THREE WAYS TO PREVENT DUPLICATES (RFC 6513, SECTION 9.1)

items.title: Discard from wrong PE
items.text: The egress PE drops packets sent by any PE other than its chosen upstream PE.

items.title: Single forwarder
items.text: An ingress PE sends into the backbone only if it is the default upstream PE selection.

items.title: Native PIM methods
items.text: With PIM over an MI-PMSI, Assert and Prune(S,G,rpt) stop steady-state duplicates.
